notes.meaning: Antiochus makes a treaty of friendship with Egypt, but he breaks his word and acts deceitfully. He begins with only a small band of troops, but he slips into the richest parts of the land without warning. Unlike previous kings, he scatters stolen riches among his followers to win their loyalty, while secretly scheming against Egypt's strongholds for as long as God allows.

Antiochus gathers a large army and marches openly against the king of the South, Ptolemy of Egypt. Even though the Egyptian king comes out with a massive force, he cannot stand his ground. He falls because his own leaders secretly plot against him.

The Egyptian king is ruined by his closest advisers, the very men who share his table and eat his food. Their betrayal causes the Egyptian army to be swept away, and great numbers of soldiers are cut down in battle.

The two kings sit at the same table pretending to make peace, but both are full of evil and tell lies to each other. Their selfish schemes accomplish nothing, because God alone controls when and how the conflict will end.

Antiochus heads back toward his own kingdom loaded with plunder from Egypt. On his journey home, his heart turns in anger against the holy covenant, and he attacks Jerusalem and steals treasures from God's temple before continuing on to Syria.
At the time God has appointed, Antiochus launches another invasion of Egypt. This expedition, however, does not end in triumph like his earlier campaigns.

Roman envoys arriving in ships from the western Mediterranean confront Antiochus and force him to turn back. Humiliated and furious, he vents his rage against God's covenant people in Jerusalem, rewarding the Jewish apostates who abandon their ancestral faith to side with him.

His soldiers defile the temple in Jerusalem, stopping the regular daily burnt offerings. In their place, they set up an idol altar dedicated to Zeus, which brings dreadful ruin and desolation to the sanctuary.

Antiochus uses smooth words and promises of reward to lead unfaithful Jews completely away from God. In contrast, those who truly know and love the Lord find spiritual strength to resist his decrees and stand firm.

Faithful teachers guide and strengthen many in the true law of God during this dark trial. Yet for remaining loyal, many of these godly believers are killed by the sword, burned alive, imprisoned, or stripped of their possessions.

When God's people suffer, the Lord sends them a little relief through the brave resistance of the Maccabees. As these fighters start to win victories, however, insincere people join their ranks just to look good or stay safe.

God permits some of these faithful leaders to suffer and die so that His people may be tested, purified, and made clean. This harsh trial will not go on forever, because God has set a definite limit to the suffering.

The arrogant ruler acts entirely as he pleases, lifting himself up above every god and shouting shocking blasphemies against the true God of heaven. He continues to succeed until the period of divine anger against Israel has run its appointed course.

differ.view: Some hold that this king represents the continuous power and arrogance of the Roman Empire rather than Antiochus alone.
Many believe the prophecy skips forward past Antiochus to describe the final, end-time Antichrist.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Historical-grammatical scholars generally maintain that the description continues without interruption to portray Antiochus Epiphanes.

notes.meaning: This ruler cares nothing for the gods his ancestors worshipped, nor for the deity loved by women, nor for any other divine power. In his extreme pride, he places himself above everything and everyone.

differ.view: Some see the lack of regard for the desire of women as a reference to the Roman Catholic ban on marriage for priests.
Many read the desire of women as the promised Messiah, whom faithful Jewish mothers longed to bear.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often identify the desire of women as an ancient Near Eastern deity like Tammuz or Adonis, whose worship was popular among women.

notes.meaning: Instead of traditional worship, he honors a god of fortresses—a symbol of military power and warfare—which his ancestors never acknowledged. He lavishes enormous wealth on this power, spending vast amounts of gold, silver, and precious stones.

differ.view: Some view the god of fortresses as referring to the veneration and costly adornment of patron saints and angels in medieval church tradition.

notes.meaning: Relying on this new god of raw power, he attacks the strongest fortified cities. He showers honors, offices, and parcels of land on those who submit to his rule and serve his interests.

At the closing stage, the king of the South attacks him, but the king of the North strikes back like a whirlwind. Marching with cavalry, chariots, and a large fleet, he rolls through many lands like an unstoppable flood.

differ.view: Some interpret these clashing northern and southern empires as the Saracen Arabs and the Ottoman Turks moving across historical lands.

notes.meaning: He marches into the Beautiful Land of Israel, bringing down many territories along the way. Yet the lands of Edom, Moab, and the leaders of Ammon manage to escape his crushing hand.

He stretches his empire over many regions, and not even the wealthy land of Egypt manages to get away. He seizes all of Egypt's hidden gold, silver, and treasures, while the Libyans and Cushites are brought under his control.
Disturbing reports from the east and the north startle and anger him. He marches out in absolute fury, fully determined to wipe out and destroy many people.
He sets up his royal tents between the Mediterranean Sea and the holy mountain in Jerusalem. Yet in the very height of his arrogance, he meets his sudden death, and not a single ally can save him.
